name: Discipline and Behavior Data
title: Discipline and Behavior Data
answer: Discipline data can reveal unfair patterns, where some groups of students are disciplined more often or more harshly than others for similar behavior. AI features in spreadsheets and student information system reports help administrators break that data down by group, school and type of offense, so the patterns show where to look more closely. It matters because a tool that looks balanced can still produce unfair results, so people must check outcomes rather than inputs.

sections.body: Discipline and behavior data is the record of who gets disciplined, how often and how harshly, and this idea is about reading that record closely enough to spot unfairness. The problem it solves is that some groups of students are disciplined more often or more harshly than others for similar behavior, and without a breakdown by group, school and type of offense those patterns stay hidden. AI features in spreadsheets and student information system reports let administrators produce those breakdowns. The patterns do not settle anything on their own, they show where to look more closely. That is the purpose of the idea, to direct attention rather than to deliver a verdict.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not sort this work by grade band, so the same routines apply across a school. Administrators use AI features in spreadsheets and student information system reports to break discipline data down by group, school and type of offense. Positive behavior intervention and support teams review data on a regular basis, looking at when and where behavior problems happen, then adjusting routines and supports. AI can chart that data and highlight patterns, but the team decides what the patterns mean. In restorative work a teacher or counselor can use AI to draft conversation scripts or questions for a restorative circle, the adult leads the conversation and adapts to the students involved, and students can practice handling conflict through role play with a school configured tool followed by discussion with an adult.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers one study and no other research. A study of test score predictions found that balancing the number of students from each group in the data did not guarantee fair predictions (Li et al., 2026). The book applies that lesson directly to discipline, noting that a tool which looks balanced can still produce unfair results, so people must check outcomes, not just inputs. Beyond that study, the guidance on discipline data, behavior review and restorative practice rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text is clear that the judgment stays with people. A chart can show a spike in problems after lunch, but it cannot say whether the cause is hunger, crowding or a single conflict, and the team has to work out what the pattern means. Fairness cannot be assumed from balanced inputs, so outcomes have to be checked rather than trusted. In restorative work the adult leads the conversation and adapts it to the students involved, and role play with a school configured tool is followed by discussion with an adult. The tool drafts and charts, the decisions remain human.
